::: {.at-a-glance}
- **Time:** Part A and Part B in class (80 minutes each), then a lab: the tasks and the GitHub check on your own project. Part C at home.
- **Slides:** [Pixi](../lectures/05-pixi/05-pixi.qmd)
- **You need:** the `ltee-project` so far: a Git repository on GitHub ([lesson 04](04-git.qmd)), with the data downloaded ([lesson 03](03-data-management.qmd#hands-on)).
- **You will have:** the LTEE pipeline running as Pixi tasks in a Linux/macOS `pipeline` environment, rebuilt and rerun by GitHub on every push; the default environment still works on every platform.
:::

## Overview

So far you have used `pixi exec` for one-off commands, and `pixi lock`
wrote a lock file for GitHub, without asking what they do. Now you open
the box. An **environment** is the set of
programs and libraries an analysis runs with. If you install them by hand,
your environment drifts: tools update, a colleague has other versions, and
results change or commands stop working. Pixi stores the environment's
*description* in the project (`pixi.toml`, written by you), records the
*exact result* (`pixi.lock`, written by Pixi), and rebuilds it anywhere.

The problem has a name, "dependency hell", and a classic answer: Conda.
Pixi uses the same packages as
Conda (from conda-forge and bioconda), but works per project, always keeps a
lock file, solves for several operating systems at once, and runs tasks. The
[Conda comparison](05b-conda-comparison.qmd) shows the Conda way side by side.

### Learning outcomes

After this lesson you can:

1. **Create** a Pixi workspace, **add** packages from conda-forge and bioconda, and **run** tools with `pixi run`.
2. **Rebuild** an environment from its lock file, and **explain** what the manifest records, what the lock file records, and what neither records.
3. **Define** tasks with dependencies that run the LTEE pipeline with one command.
4. **Make** a project work across platforms by putting tools that exist only for Linux and macOS in a separate feature and environment.
5. **Install** a personal command-line tool with `pixi global`, and (optional) run a Pixi project on an HPC cluster.

Checks: `pixi install --locked` rebuilds your environment from a clean state
(outcome 2); `pixi run reproduce` runs the pipeline (3, 4); the *Reproduce*
GitHub Action runs it on a fresh machine and is green on your pull request
(2 to 4).

# Part A: how Pixi works

## 1. The problem in two commands

FastQC is the first tool of our pipeline. Version 0.12.1 has an option `-o`
for the output folder. Version 0.13.0, released in 2026, replaced FastQC's
launcher and `-o` is gone (only `--outdir` is left). Compare the help of both,
each run in a temporary environment with `pixi exec`:

```{.bash .run}
pixi exec -c conda-forge -c bioconda --spec "fastqc==0.12.1" -- fastqc --help | grep -e "--outdir"
pixi exec -c conda-forge -c bioconda --spec "fastqc==0.13.0" -- fastqc --help | grep -e "--outdir"
```

```text
    -o --outdir     Create all output files in the specified output directory.
  --outdir OUTDIR       Create all output files in the specified output
```

A script that ran `fastqc -o results/` worked last year and fails today with
`fastqc: error: unrecognized arguments: -o`. Nothing in your script changed:
the environment did. (This happened to us while writing this course.)

## 2. A practice workspace: manifest and lock file

Pixi is already installed ([lesson 00](00-setup.qmd)). Make a small practice
workspace next to your project:

```{.bash .run}
cd ~/cbio7501
pixi init pixi-practice -c conda-forge -c bioconda
cd pixi-practice
ls -a
cat pixi.toml
```

```toml
[workspace]
channels = ["conda-forge", "bioconda"]
name = "pixi-practice"
platforms = ["osx-arm64"]
version = "0.1.0"

[tasks]

[dependencies]
```

`pixi.toml` is the **manifest**: what you want. `channels` are where packages
come from ([conda-forge](https://conda-forge.org/) for general software,
[bioconda](https://bioconda.github.io/) for bioinformatics; order matters,
first wins). `platforms` lists the operating systems the environment must
work on; Pixi filled in yours (`linux-64`, `osx-arm64`, `osx-64` or `win-64`).

Add samtools:

```{.bash .run}
pixi add samtools
ls -a
```

```text
✔ Added samtools >=1.24,<2
```

Three things happened:

- `pixi.toml` now says `samtools = ">=1.24,<2"`: any 1.x from 1.24 on. That is
  your intent, written by you (through `pixi add`).
- `pixi.lock` appeared: the **lock file**. It lists the *exact* package, build,
  download URL and checksum of samtools **and of every one of its
  dependencies**, for each platform. Written by Pixi, never by hand.
- `.pixi/envs/default/` holds the installed environment. It can be deleted at
  any time; the lock file rebuilds it.

Look at the lock file and the full environment:

```{.bash .run}
grep -m 3 "samtools" pixi.lock
pixi list
pixi tree samtools
```

You asked for one package; the environment has dozens (`htslib`, `zlib`, ...).
The lock file pins all of them.

## 3. `pixi run` and `pixi shell`

```{.bash .run}
pixi run samtools --version | head -1
samtools --version || echo "samtools is not on PATH outside the environment"
```

`pixi run CMD` runs one command inside the environment, then leaves it. The
second line shows that samtools is not installed "on your laptop"; it is
installed in the project.

`pixi shell` starts a new shell *inside* the environment, until you type
`exit`. Handy for interactive work; `pixi run` is better in scripts, tasks
and on clusters.

```{.bash .norun}
pixi shell
samtools --version
exit
```

## 4. Prove it: rebuild from the lock file

Delete the environment and rebuild it **from the lock file only**:

```{.bash .run}
pixi clean
ls .pixi/envs 2>/dev/null || echo "no environments left"
pixi install --locked
pixi run samtools --version | head -1
```

`--locked` means: install exactly what `pixi.lock` says, and stop with an error
if the lock file does not match the manifest. This is what the GitHub Action
does (`locked: true`), and what a colleague does after cloning your project.
The second install is fast because Pixi keeps downloaded packages in a cache.

## 5. Break it: change a version on purpose

Your reviewer asks you to rerun with samtools 1.21. Keep a copy of the lock
file and change the requirement:

```{.bash .run}
cp pixi.lock pixi.lock.before
pixi add "samtools==1.21"
grep "samtools" pixi.toml
diff pixi.lock.before pixi.lock | grep -E "samtools-|htslib-"
pixi run samtools --version | head -1
```

```text
samtools = "==1.21"
<       - conda: https://conda.anaconda.org/bioconda/osx-arm64/htslib-1.24-hd3c6ec9_0.conda
<       - conda: https://conda.anaconda.org/bioconda/osx-arm64/samtools-1.24-h36b3a25_2.conda
>       - conda: https://conda.anaconda.org/bioconda/osx-arm64/htslib-1.21-hfcd771d_1.tar.bz2
>       - conda: https://conda.anaconda.org/bioconda/osx-arm64/samtools-1.21-h267f7b9_1.tar.bz2
samtools 1.21
```

One line in the manifest changed two packages in the lock file (samtools
pulled its matching htslib down with it). Every change to the manifest updates
the lock file, so the lock file always describes what you actually ran. Now
try to install the *old* lock file against the *new* manifest:

```{.bash .expect-fail}
cp pixi.lock.before pixi.lock
pixi install --locked
```

```text
Error:   × lock file not up-to-date with the workspace
```

`--locked` refuses: the lock file and the manifest disagree. Without
`--locked`, Pixi would simply solve again and update the lock file. Restore and
clean up:

```{.bash .run}
pixi add "samtools>=1.24"
rm pixi.lock.before
cd ~/cbio7501
```

::: {.callout-note title="What the lock file does *not* pin"}
- **Hardware and the operating system.** Packages are built for a platform
  and rely on the system's C library (on Linux, `glibc`; `pixi info` shows it
  as a "virtual package"). A very old cluster can be too old for new packages.
- **The data.** That is what `metadata/checksums.sha256` is for.
- **The channels themselves.** A package can be removed from a channel, or a
  channel can disappear. For long-term reproducibility, also archive a
  container image ([lesson 08](08-containers.qmd)).
- **Randomness and threads.** Same software, different seed or thread count,
  can still give different results ([lesson 09](09-snakemake.qmd)).
:::

# Part B: the LTEE pipeline as Pixi tasks

## 6. Add the pipeline tools, and hit Windows

Go to the project and start a branch for this lesson:

```{.bash .run}
cd ~/cbio7501/ltee-project
```

```{.bash .run-ci}
git switch -c lesson-05-pixi
```

Your project's manifest lists four platforms, because the template wants
reports and notebooks (lessons 07 and 06) to work on Windows too:

```{.bash .run}
grep platforms pixi.toml
```

Add the pipeline tools (FastQC, MultiQC, BWA, samtools, bcftools):

```{.bash .expect-fail}
pixi add fastqc multiqc bwa samtools bcftools
```

```text
Error:   × failed to solve requirements of environment 'default' for platform 'win-64'
  ╰─▶ Cannot solve the request because of: No candidates were found for bwa *.
```

Pixi solves for **every** platform in the list, and `bwa`, `samtools` and
`bcftools` have no Windows builds (we checked on 2026-10-24: Linux and macOS
builds exist on bioconda, Windows ones do not). Pixi tells you *now*, on your
Mac or Linux laptop, instead of a Windows colleague finding out next month.

You have two honest options: drop `win-64` from the project (Windows users
work in WSL2, which is Linux), or keep reports and notebooks working on Windows and put
the pipeline tools in a part of the project that only exists on Linux and
macOS. We do the second, with a **feature**.

## 7. Features and environments

A **feature** is a named piece of an environment: its own dependencies, tasks
and, if needed, platforms. An **environment** combines features. Every
environment includes the default feature (the top-level `[dependencies]`)
unless you say otherwise.

Create a `pipeline` feature for Linux and macOS, an environment that uses it,
and add the tools to it:

```{.bash .run}
pixi workspace platform add --feature pipeline linux-64 osx-arm64 osx-64
pixi workspace environment add pipeline --feature pipeline
pixi add --feature pipeline fastqc multiqc bwa samtools bcftools
```

```text
✔ Added fastqc >=0.13.0,<0.14
✔ Added multiqc >=1.35,<2
✔ Added bwa >=0.7.19,<0.8
✔ Added samtools >=1.24,<2
✔ Added bcftools >=1.24,<2
Added these only for feature: pipeline
```

The end of `pixi.toml` now reads:

```toml
[feature.pipeline]
platforms = ["linux-64", "osx-arm64", "osx-64"]

[feature.pipeline.dependencies]
fastqc = ">=0.13.0,<0.14"
multiqc = ">=1.35,<2"
bwa = ">=0.7.19,<0.8"
samtools = ">=1.24,<2"
bcftools = ">=1.24,<2"

[environments]
pipeline = ["pipeline"]
```

So the project has two environments:

| Environment | Contains | Platforms |
|-------------|----------|-----------|
| `default` | Python, Quarto, Jupyter, pandas, matplotlib, papermill | Linux, macOS, Windows |
| `pipeline` | everything in `default` **plus** the pipeline tools | Linux, macOS |

Run a tool in a named environment with `-e`:

```{.bash .run}
pixi run -e pipeline samtools --version | head -1
pixi run -e pipeline fastqc --version
```

## 8. Tasks for the pipeline

A **task** is a named command stored in `pixi.toml`, so nobody has to remember
long commands. The template defined two: `check` and a placeholder
`reproduce`. List them, then make the data download from lesson 03 a task:

```{.bash .run}
pixi task list
pixi task add download "python scripts/download_data.py" --description "Download the raw data and verify checksums"
pixi run download
```

```text
✨ Pixi task (download in default): python scripts/download_data.py
OK: all 7 raw files present, sha256 verified, read-only
```

The first `pixi run` in the project installs its default environment (a few
minutes, once). The task works the same for everyone: no need to remember the
script's name or which Python to use.

### Quality control

Run FastQC on every FASTQ file, then MultiQC to combine the reports. The task
belongs to the `pipeline` feature, because it needs its tools, and it depends
on `download`, so the data is always there and checked first:

```{.bash .run}
pixi task add --feature pipeline qc "mkdir -p results/qc/fastqc && fastqc --quiet --threads 2 --outdir results/qc/fastqc data/raw/fastq/*.fastq && multiqc --force -o results/qc/multiqc results/qc/fastqc" --depends-on download --description "FastQC on each FASTQ file, then a MultiQC summary"
pixi run qc
```

```text
✨ Pixi task (download in default): python scripts/download_data.py
OK: all 7 raw files present, sha256 verified, read-only

✨ Pixi task (qc in pipeline): mkdir -p results/qc/fastqc && fastqc ...
...
     multiqc | MultiQC complete
```

Notice `download in default` and `qc in pipeline`: Pixi picks, for each task,
the environment that has it. Open `results/qc/multiqc/multiqc_report.html`.
The reads were trimmed before they were shared, so expect a clean report:
that is a property of this teaching data, not something to expect from raw
sequencing data.

::: {.callout-note title="Task commands run in Pixi's own shell"}
Tasks run in a small cross-platform shell built into Pixi. It understands
`&&`, `|`, `>` and wildcards like `*.fastq` on every operating system, but not
Bash loops or `if`. For anything longer, write a script and make the task run
it, as in the next step.
:::

### Alignment and variant calling

These steps follow the Data Carpentry *Wrangling Genomics* lesson exactly. It
automates them with a shell script; we use the same script, with paths
relative to the project folder. Save it as `scripts/run_variant_calling.sh`:

```{.bash filename="scripts/run_variant_calling.sh" .write}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Variant calling for the LTEE subset, one sample after another.
#
# Adapted from Data Carpentry "Wrangling Genomics", episode "Automating a
# Variant Calling Workflow" (run_variant_calling.sh), CC BY 4.0,
# https://datacarpentry.github.io/wrangling-genomics/05-automation.html
# Changes: paths are relative to the project folder, the reference is taken
# from data/raw/ and decompressed into data/processed/, alignment and variant
# statistics are added, and the minimum read depth of the final filter (the
# analysis question) and the output folder are parameters. Tool options are
# the lesson's.
#
# Usage (from the project folder):
#   bash scripts/run_variant_calling.sh [MIN_DEPTH] [OUTPUT_FOLDER]
set -euo pipefail

min_depth=${1:-2}   # vcfutils.pl varFilter -d (2 is its default)
out=${2:-results}   # all results go below this folder

genome=data/processed/reference/ecoli_rel606.fasta
mkdir -p data/processed/reference "$out/sam" "$out/bam" "$out/bcf" "$out/vcf" "$out/stats"

if [ ! -s "$genome" ]; then
    gunzip -c data/raw/reference/ecoli_rel606.fasta.gz > "$genome"
fi
bwa index "$genome"

for fq1 in data/raw/fastq/*_1.trim.sub.fastq; do
    base=$(basename "$fq1" _1.trim.sub.fastq)
    echo "working on sample $base"

    fq2=data/raw/fastq/${base}_2.trim.sub.fastq
    sam=$out/sam/${base}.aligned.sam
    bam=$out/bam/${base}.aligned.bam
    sorted_bam=$out/bam/${base}.aligned.sorted.bam
    raw_bcf=$out/bcf/${base}_raw.bcf
    variants=$out/bcf/${base}_variants.vcf
    final_variants=$out/vcf/${base}_final_variants.vcf

    bwa mem "$genome" "$fq1" "$fq2" > "$sam"
    samtools view -S -b "$sam" > "$bam"
    samtools sort -o "$sorted_bam" "$bam"
    samtools index "$sorted_bam"
    samtools flagstat "$sorted_bam" > "$out/stats/${base}.flagstat.txt"
    bcftools mpileup -O b -o "$raw_bcf" -f "$genome" "$sorted_bam"
    bcftools call --ploidy 1 -m -v -o "$variants" "$raw_bcf"
    vcfutils.pl varFilter -d "$min_depth" "$variants" > "$final_variants"
    bcftools stats "$final_variants" > "$out/stats/${base}.bcftools-stats.txt"
done

echo "done: final variants in $out/vcf/"
```

You do not need to know the genomics: the script indexes the reference,
aligns each sample's reads (`bwa mem`), converts and sorts the alignments
(`samtools`), calls variants (`bcftools mpileup` and `call`, haploid) and
filters them (`vcfutils.pl varFilter`, which comes with bcftools). Make it a
task and run it (about a minute on a laptop):

```{.bash .run}
pixi task add --feature pipeline variant-calling "bash scripts/run_variant_calling.sh" --depends-on download --description "Align, call and filter variants (shell script)"
pixi run variant-calling
```

Count the variants per sample:

```{.bash .run}
for f in results/vcf/*_final_variants.vcf; do echo "$f $(grep -vc '^#' "$f")"; done
```

```text
results/vcf/SRR2584863_final_variants.vcf 25
results/vcf/SRR2584866_final_variants.vcf 775
results/vcf/SRR2589044_final_variants.vcf 10
```

The Data Carpentry lesson reports 10, 25 and 766 with the tool versions of
2018. Two samples match exactly; the hypermutator clone (SRR2584866, 50,000
generations) differs by 9 variants out of about 770. Same data, same commands,
newer software: a small but real difference. This is why the versions go
into the lock file (and, from lesson 07, into the report).

### One command for everything

Make `reproduce` run the whole analysis, so the GitHub Action does too:

```{.bash .run}
pixi task remove reproduce
pixi task alias reproduce qc variant-calling
pixi task list
pixi run reproduce
```

`pixi run reproduce` downloads and checks the data (once), then runs QC and
variant calling in the `pipeline` environment. The report joins in lesson 07.

### Save your work, and let GitHub reproduce it

The lock file changed (new environment, new packages). Commit it with the
manifest and the script, push, and open a pull request:

```{.bash .run-ci}
git add pixi.toml pixi.lock scripts/run_variant_calling.sh
git commit -m "Run QC and variant calling as Pixi tasks in a pipeline environment"
git push -u origin lesson-05-pixi
```

In lesson 04 the *Reproduce* check had nothing to do. Now open the pull
request and click the check's *Details*: on a Linux machine that has never
seen your project, GitHub clones the repository, rebuilds both environments
from `pixi.lock`, downloads the data from figshare and NCBI, checks the
checksums, and runs QC and variant calling. A green check means your project
**reproduces from a clean clone**. Merge the pull request.

::: {.callout-tip title="If the check fails"}
Read the log from the bottom up. Common causes: a file you use is not
committed (`git status` on your laptop shows it as untracked), a path that
only exists on your laptop, or `pixi.lock` out of date with `pixi.toml`
(run `pixi install` and commit `pixi.lock`).
:::

Merge locally if you are not using GitHub (or in the course tests):

```{.bash .run-ci}
git switch main
git merge lesson-05-pixi
git push
```

# Part C: beyond one project

## 9. Personal tools with `pixi global`

Some tools are not part of any project: Git, a nicer `cat`, Cookiecutter.
`pixi global install` gives each one its own small environment and puts the
command on your `PATH`, without touching your projects:

```{.bash .run}
pixi global install cookiecutter
pixi global list
```

```{.bash .norun}
cookiecutter --version     # works in any folder (open a new terminal first)
```

Upgrade with `pixi global update`, remove with `pixi global uninstall cookiecutter`.

## 10. Pixi on an HPC cluster (optional, for Karakoram users)

Pixi needs no administrator rights, so it works on clusters:

- **Install** it in your home folder with the same one-line installer.
- **Cache and quota.** Pixi's package cache grows to several GB. If your home
  quota is small, point the cache at project storage before installing, for
  example `export PIXI_CACHE_DIR=/path/to/project/space/pixi-cache` in your
  `~/.bashrc` (ask your admins which file system to use).
- **Run through the scheduler** with `pixi run`, as in Amrei Binzer-Panchal's
  course: `srun -A <project> -t 00:30:00 -n 1 pixi run qc`. In a batch script,
  `cd` to the project folder and call `pixi run ...`.
- **`pixi shell` may not work** on some clusters' login setups; `pixi run`
  always does.
- **Compute nodes without internet:** run `pixi install --locked` on the login
  node first; the job then needs no downloads.
- **Same lock file, other platform:** your laptop is `osx-arm64`, the cluster
  is `linux-64`. Because the manifest lists both, the lock file already has the
  exact Linux packages: nothing is solved again on the cluster.

## 11. How does this compare with Conda?

If you have used Conda or Mamba, see the [Conda comparison](05b-conda-comparison.qmd):
a command table, converting an `environment.yml` with `pixi init --import`,
exporting a Pixi environment for Conda users, and an honest list of where
Conda is still fine.

## 12. Did it reproduce?

Swap with a neighbor. Clone their repository and run their analysis on your
laptop:

```{.bash .norun}
cd ~/cbio7501
git clone git@github.com:NEIGHBOR/ltee-project.git neighbor-ltee
cd neighbor-ltee
pixi run reproduce
```

Did it work without asking them anything? Compare your variant counts. If it
failed, open an issue on their repository with the error message: that is
exactly the feedback a reviewer would give.

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | What to do |
|---------|------------|
| `No candidates were found for bwa` (or samtools, bcftools) | You added it to the default feature, which includes `win-64`. Use `--feature pipeline` (step 7). |
| `lock file not up-to-date with the workspace` | Someone changed `pixi.toml` without updating `pixi.lock`. Run `pixi install` (without `--locked`) and commit `pixi.lock`. |
| `the environment directory has moved from ... to ...` | You moved or renamed the project folder. Environments cannot move: `rm -rf .pixi/envs` and run your command again; Pixi rebuilds from the lock file. |
| `fastqc: error: unrecognized arguments: -o` | FastQC 0.13 dropped `-o`; use `--outdir` (step 1). |
| A task with a loop or `if` fails with a syntax error | Pixi's task shell is not Bash. Put the logic in a script and run the script from the task. |
| `pixi run reproduce` fails on native Windows | Expected: the `pipeline` environment does not exist on Windows. Use WSL2 or Codespaces. |
| Downloads are slow in class | Run `pixi install --all` at home; the cache makes later installs fast. |
| Disk is full | `pixi clean` removes this project's environments; `pixi clean cache` empties the shared cache ([B Take-down](B-take-down.qmd)). |

## Apply it to your own mini-analysis

In your own project: add the tools your analysis needs with `pixi add` (use a
feature if a tool is missing on a platform you list), make your steps tasks,
and make `reproduce` run them all. Commit `pixi.toml` and `pixi.lock`, push,
and get the *Reproduce* check green.

## Key points

- `pixi.toml` is what you ask for; `pixi.lock` is exactly what you got, for every platform. Commit both.
- `pixi run` runs a command in the project's environment; `pixi install --locked` rebuilds it exactly.
- Every manifest change updates the lock file; old versions can be restored on purpose.
- A lock file pins packages, not hardware, data, channels or randomness.
- Features and environments keep platform-specific tools apart; tasks pick the right environment.
- Tasks turn long commands into one word; `reproduce` runs everything.

## Further reading

- Cheat sheet: [Pixi](../cheatsheets/pixi.qmd), with links to the official cheat sheets and references.
- Pixi documentation: <https://pixi.prefix.dev/latest/>, in particular *Multi environment* (<https://pixi.prefix.dev/latest/workspace/multi_environment/>), *Tasks* (<https://pixi.prefix.dev/latest/workspace/advanced_tasks/>) and *Global tools* (<https://pixi.prefix.dev/latest/global_tools/introduction/>).
- The Carpentries Incubator, *Introduction to Pixi*: <https://carpentries-incubator.github.io/pixi-introduction/>
- Amrei Binzer-Panchal, *Reproducible Research* course, Pixi pages: <https://amrei-bp.github.io/Reproducible_Research/course_environments.html>
- NBIS, *Conda* tutorial (with its Pixi extra section): <https://nbisweden.github.io/workshop-reproducible-research/pages/conda.html>
- Grüning B et al. (2018). Bioconda: sustainable and comprehensive software distribution for the life sciences. *Nat Methods* 15:475–476. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-018-0046-7>
